items.title: A client with crushing substernal pressure has diaphoresis and nausea. The pain began 20 minutes ago. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
items.content: Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly.
items.rationale: A rapid ECG identifies ischemic changes and supports time-sensitive acute coronary syndrome treatment. Do not delay assessment for routine tasks.

items.title: A client develops sudden aphasia and right arm weakness while eating breakfast. Which information is most important to establish immediately?
items.content: The exact time the client was last known to be at baseline.
items.rationale: Last-known-well time determines eligibility for time-dependent stroke interventions. Activate the stroke response and obtain urgent brain imaging.

items.title: A client with chronic kidney disease has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves. Which prescribed intervention should the nurse anticipate first to stabilize the myocardium?
items.content: IV calcium gluconate.
items.rationale: IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes. It does not lower serum potassium, so potassium-shifting and removal therapies are also required.

items.title: A client with heart failure is sitting upright, gasping, and producing pink frothy sputum. SpO₂ is 82%. Which action is the priority?
items.content: Activate emergency assistance and support oxygenation while preparing prescribed ventilatory support.
items.rationale: Severe hypoxemia and pulmonary edema are immediately life-threatening. Rapid escalation and respiratory support take priority while prescribed therapies are prepared.

items.title: A client is prescribed insulin lispro before meals. The meal tray is delayed and the insulin has not yet been administered. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Wait until the meal is available and coordinate administration with food intake.
items.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin has an early onset. Giving it without food increases hypoglycemia risk; coordinate administration with the meal and prescription.

items.title: Before administering digoxin to an adult, the nurse notes an apical pulse of 52/min and new nausea. What is the best action?
items.content: Withhold the dose and notify the prescriber.
items.rationale: Bradycardia and new gastrointestinal symptoms may indicate digoxin effect or toxicity. Withhold and obtain further assessment, including potassium, renal function, and drug level as ordered.

items.title: Immediately after rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate falls to 70/min and a loop of cord is visible. What should the nurse do first?
items.content: Call for emergency assistance and manually elevate the presenting part off the cord.
items.rationale: Cord compression compromises fetal oxygenation. Relieve pressure on the cord, position to reduce compression, and prepare for emergency birth.

items.title: During birth, the fetal head delivers and then retracts against the perineum. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
items.content: Assist with the McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure as directed.
items.rationale: The turtle sign suggests shoulder dystocia. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure are first-line maneuvers; fundal pressure is contraindicated.

items.title: A 4-year-old has drooling, a muffled voice, tripod positioning, and inspiratory stridor. Which action should the nurse avoid?
items.content: Inspecting the throat with a tongue depressor.
items.rationale: Throat manipulation can precipitate complete airway obstruction in suspected epiglottitis. Keep the child calm and obtain expert airway support.

items.title: A client with acute mania is pacing, interrupting others, and has eaten very little. Which intervention is most appropriate?
items.content: Offer frequent high-calorie finger foods and fluids in a low-stimulation setting.
items.rationale: Finger foods support intake when sitting for meals is difficult. Reduce stimulation and provide concise limits and close safety monitoring.

items.title: Fifteen minutes after a transfusion begins, a client reports chills and flank pain. What should the nurse do immediately?
items.content: Stop the transfusion.
items.rationale: Chills and flank pain may indicate an acute hemolytic reaction. Stop the blood product, maintain IV access with normal saline using new tubing, assess, and notify the team and blood bank.

items.title: A chest drainage system becomes disconnected from the chest tube. Which immediate action should the nurse take?
items.content: Place the end of the chest tube in sterile water while obtaining a new drainage system.
items.rationale: A temporary sterile-water seal limits air entry into the pleural space. Re-establish a closed drainage system promptly and assess respiratory status.

items.title: A client receiving IV unfractionated heparin develops hematuria and a markedly elevated aPTT. What is the priority nursing action?
items.content: Stop the infusion and notify the prescriber immediately.
items.rationale: Active bleeding with excessive anticoagulation requires stopping heparin and urgent evaluation. Protamine may be prescribed for reversal depending on severity.

items.title: A client with suspected infection has BP 82/44 mm Hg, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, and altered mentation. Which action is most appropriate?
items.content: Initiate the sepsis response and administer prescribed crystalloid resuscitation promptly.
items.rationale: Hypotension, elevated lactate, and altered mentation indicate impaired perfusion. Rapid protocol-based resuscitation, cultures when feasible without delaying antimicrobials, and antibiotics are time-critical.

items.title: A client receiving hemodialysis reports that the usual vibration over the fistula is absent. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Notify the dialysis team immediately and avoid using the access until evaluated.
items.rationale: An absent thrill may indicate thrombosis or access occlusion. Prompt evaluation is needed; do not compress, puncture, or use the access.

items.title: A client with COPD has increased dyspnea, purulent sputum, and wheezing. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Position upright; administer prescribed short-acting bronchodilator; titrate prescribed oxygen to the individualized target; reassess work of breathing and oxygenation.
items.rationale: Upright positioning improves ventilation. Bronchodilation and carefully titrated oxygen treat exacerbation and hypoxemia. Reassessment detects fatigue or deterioration; oxygen should not be withheld.

items.title: A client is starting lisinopril. Which findings should the nurse teach the client to report promptly? Select all that apply.
items.content: Swelling of the lips or tongue; persistent troublesome cough; dizziness or fainting.
items.rationale: Angioedema is an emergency, cough is a recognized adverse effect, and symptomatic hypotension needs evaluation. Do not stop or change therapy without prescriber guidance unless emergency instructions apply.

items.title: A postpartum client has a boggy fundus, heavy lochia, and a rising heart rate. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
items.content: Massage the fundus; call for assistance; quantify blood loss and assess vital signs; prepare prescribed uterotonic medication.
items.rationale: Uterine atony is a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Immediate fundal massage, escalation, quantified blood loss, hemodynamic assessment, and uterotonics are appropriate.

items.title: An infant has vomiting and diarrhea. Which findings support significant dehydration? Select all that apply.
items.content: Sunken fontanel; capillary refill of 4 seconds; markedly decreased wet diapers; lethargy.
items.rationale: These findings indicate reduced circulating volume and possible impaired perfusion. Assess severity promptly and initiate prescribed rehydration and monitoring.

items.title: A client states, “I have the pills at home and plan to take them tonight.” Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Ask directly about intent and access; maintain continuous observation per policy; remove access to potential means in the care setting; arrange urgent psychiatric evaluation.
items.rationale: A specific plan, means, and near-term timing indicate imminent risk. Direct assessment, observation, means safety, and urgent team escalation are required; do not promise secrecy.

items.title: A client has suspected C. difficile diarrhea. Which infection-control actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Use gown and gloves on room entry; wash hands with soap and water; dedicate equipment when possible; use an approved sporicidal environmental disinfectant.
items.rationale: Contact precautions and spore-focused environmental cleaning are required. Soap-and-water handwashing is preferred because alcohol hand rub does not reliably remove spores.

items.title: A client with acute pancreatitis has severe epigastric pain and vomiting. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Administer prescribed IV fluids; provide prescribed analgesia; monitor glucose and electrolytes; maintain prescribed bowel rest during severe symptoms.
items.rationale: Fluid resuscitation, pain control, and monitoring for metabolic complications are central. Oral intake is individualized and restarted as tolerated rather than prolonged automatically.

items.title: A client taking lithium reports diarrhea and develops coarse tremor and unsteady gait. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Withhold lithium pending urgent prescriber direction; assess neurologic status and hydration; obtain serum lithium and renal/electrolyte studies as ordered.
items.rationale: Gastrointestinal symptoms with coarse tremor and ataxia suggest toxicity. Hold further doses pending urgent review and evaluate level, renal function, electrolytes, and volume status.

items.title: A postoperative client suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and SpO₂ 86%. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Activate rapid response; provide oxygen as prescribed; keep the client at rest; prepare for urgent diagnostic evaluation and anticoagulation if prescribed.
items.rationale: Acute pulmonary embolism can cause rapid hemodynamic compromise. Escalation, oxygenation, minimizing exertion, and urgent evaluation are priorities.

items.title: A pregnant client at 34 weeks has BP 168/112 mm Hg, severe headache, and visual spots. Which actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Institute seizure precautions; notify the obstetric team urgently; administer prescribed magnesium sulfate; prepare prescribed rapid-acting antihypertensive therapy.
items.rationale: Severe-range hypertension with neurologic symptoms is an obstetric emergency. Magnesium prevents seizures, while antihypertensive treatment reduces maternal stroke risk.

items.title: Twenty minutes after IV hydromorphone, a client is difficult to arouse, has RR 7/min, and SpO₂ 86%. Select the 3 priority nursing actions.
items.content: Support airway and ventilation; activate urgent clinical assistance; prepare and administer prescribed naloxone according to protocol.
items.rationale: The client has opioid-induced respiratory depression. Airway and ventilatory support, immediate escalation, and naloxone when indicated address the immediate threat; reassess for recurrent sedation.

items.title: A client with septic shock has falling urine output and rising creatinine. Select the 3 assessments most useful for evaluating renal perfusion and injury.
items.content: Hourly urine output; serial serum creatinine and electrolytes; blood pressure and perfusion trend.
items.rationale: Urine output and creatinine trends identify worsening kidney function, while hemodynamic data help assess perfusion. Interpret findings with fluid balance and clinical status.

items.title: A school-age child has severe asthma symptoms. Select the 3 findings that indicate impending respiratory failure.
items.content: Silent or markedly diminished breath sounds; decreasing level of consciousness; exhaustion with decreasing respiratory effort.
items.rationale: A silent chest may reflect critically poor airflow. Altered consciousness and exhaustion signal respiratory muscle fatigue and impending failure, requiring emergency escalation.

items.title: The RN is assigning care for stable clients. Select the 3 tasks appropriate for trained UAP personnel.
items.content: Obtain routine vital signs for a stable client; assist a stable client with bathing; record oral intake for a client without swallowing precautions.
items.rationale: Predictable, routine tasks may be delegated with clear directions and follow-up. Assessment, clinical judgment, teaching, and evaluation remain RN responsibilities.

items.title: A client with traumatic brain injury is being monitored. Select the 3 findings most concerning for rising intracranial pressure.
items.content: Declining level of consciousness; new unequal pupils; repeated vomiting with worsening headache.
items.rationale: A change in consciousness is often an early sensitive sign. Pupillary changes and worsening headache/vomiting suggest neurologic deterioration and require urgent escalation.

items.title: Match each medication with the adverse effect that requires urgent follow-up.
items.content: rows:digoxin;warfarin;gentamicin|columns:bradycardia with visual halos;melena with weakness;new tinnitus and rising creatinine|answers:digoxin=bradycardia with visual halos;warfarin=melena with weakness;gentamicin=new tinnitus and rising creatinine
items.rationale: Digoxin toxicity can cause bradycardia and visual disturbances. Warfarin-associated gastrointestinal bleeding may present as melena and weakness. Gentamicin can cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

items.title: Match each laboratory result with its most likely immediate risk.
items.content: rows:K 2.7 mEq/L;Na 118 mEq/L;Ca 7.1 mg/dL|columns:ventricular dysrhythmia;seizure from cerebral edema;tetany and laryngospasm|answers:K 2.7 mEq/L=ventricular dysrhythmia;Na 118 mEq/L=seizure from cerebral edema;Ca 7.1 mg/dL=tetany and laryngospasm
items.rationale: Severe hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk. Severe hyponatremia can cause cerebral edema and seizures. Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause tetany or laryngospasm.

items.title: For each condition, select all appropriate precautions or controls.
items.content: rows:pulmonary tuberculosis;C. difficile;influenza|columns:airborne isolation;fit-tested respirator;gown and gloves;soap-and-water hand hygiene;droplet precautions|answers:pulmonary tuberculosis=airborne isolation,fit-tested respirator;C. difficile=gown and gloves,soap-and-water hand hygiene;influenza=droplet precautions
items.rationale: Tuberculosis requires airborne isolation and fit-tested respiratory protection. C. difficile requires contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene. Influenza generally requires droplet precautions.

items.title: For each fetal monitoring finding, select all appropriate interpretations or responses.
items.content: rows:recurrent late decelerations;recurrent variable decelerations;prolonged deceleration|columns:uteroplacental insufficiency concern;cord compression concern;immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation|answers:recurrent late decelerations=uteroplacental insufficiency concern,immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation;recurrent variable decelerations=cord compression concern,immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation;prolonged deceleration=immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation
items.rationale: Late decelerations suggest impaired uteroplacental exchange; variable decelerations commonly reflect cord compression. A prolonged deceleration requires immediate assessment and corrective measures while preparing escalation.

items.title: Complete the initial DKA safety plan: begin prescribed ___ resuscitation; check serum ___ before insulin; if potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L, replace potassium and ___ insulin temporarily.
items.content: isotonic crystalloid|potassium|delay
items.rationale: DKA causes profound volume depletion and total-body potassium loss. Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly; severe hypokalemia must be corrected before insulin is initiated to reduce dysrhythmia risk.

items.title: A client taking warfarin should keep dietary vitamin K intake ___, report ___ stools promptly, and avoid starting NSAIDs without prescriber advice because of increased ___ risk.
items.content: consistent|black tarry|bleeding
items.rationale: Stable vitamin K intake supports predictable anticoagulation. Melena may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding. NSAIDs increase bleeding risk when combined with warfarin.

items.title: A client with pneumonia has fever, confusion, BP 78/42 mm Hg, and lactate 5.1 mmol/L. Select the likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:septic shock|actions:obtain blood cultures if this does not delay antimicrobials;administer prescribed broad-spectrum antimicrobials promptly|monitor:mean arterial pressure;serum lactate trend
items.rationale: Hypotension, altered mentation, infection, and elevated lactate indicate septic shock with impaired perfusion. Cultures should not delay antimicrobials. MAP and lactate trends help evaluate perfusion and response.

items.title: A client 30 minutes after birth has a boggy uterus, heavy bleeding, HR 128/min, and BP 86/50 mm Hg. Select the likely condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:uterine atony with postpartum hemorrhage|actions:perform fundal massage and summon help;prepare prescribed uterotonic and IV resuscitation|monitor:quantified blood loss;heart rate and blood pressure trend
items.rationale: A boggy uterus with heavy bleeding and hemodynamic changes indicates postpartum hemorrhage, commonly from atony. Immediate uterine massage, escalation, uterotonics, resuscitation, and quantified monitoring are essential.

items.title: Highlight the findings that indicate a possible acute stroke: sudden facial asymmetry; chronic bilateral knee pain; new slurred speech; unilateral arm drift; longstanding corrected visual acuity.
items.content: segments:sudden facial asymmetry|chronic bilateral knee pain|new slurred speech|unilateral arm drift|longstanding corrected visual acuity|correct:1,3,4
items.rationale: Sudden facial asymmetry, speech disturbance, and unilateral weakness are focal neurologic deficits. Activate the stroke pathway and establish last-known-well time.

items.title: Highlight the findings that require immediate escalation in a child with respiratory illness: nasal flaring; mild clear rhinorrhea; intercostal retractions; SpO₂ 87% on room air; playful behavior between coughing episodes.
items.content: segments:nasal flaring|mild clear rhinorrhea|intercostal retractions|SpO2 87% on room air|playful behavior between coughing episodes|correct:1,3,4
items.rationale: Nasal flaring, retractions, and hypoxemia indicate increased work of breathing and impaired oxygenation. The child needs prompt respiratory assessment and escalation.

items.title: A child weighs 16 kg. The prescribed medication dose is 12 mg/kg per dose. Calculate the dose in mg.
items.rationale: 12 mg/kg × 16 kg = 192 mg per dose. Verify the medication’s maximum dose, concentration, and safe pediatric dosing range before administration.

items.title: A prescription is to infuse 1,000 mL over 8 hours using an electronic pump. What rate should the nurse program in mL/hr?
items.rationale: 1,000 mL ÷ 8 hours = 125 mL/hr. Verify the order, fluid, access, and pump settings independently according to policy.

items.title: Place the actions in order for a client who develops fever, chills, and back pain during a red blood cell transfusion.
items.content: Stop the transfusion.|Keep IV access open with normal saline using new tubing.|Assess vital signs and notify the provider and blood bank.|Send the blood product and obtain ordered specimens per policy.
items.rationale: Stopping the transfusion is the first action. Maintain access with new tubing and saline, assess and notify the team, then complete the reaction workup and documentation.

items.title: A client with suspected acute coronary syndrome reports ongoing chest pressure. Select all appropriate immediate nursing actions.
items.content: Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly.|Assess vital signs and oxygenation.|Establish IV access and obtain ordered cardiac biomarkers.|Administer prescribed antiplatelet therapy after checking contraindications.|Encourage the client to walk to reduce anxiety.
items.rationale: Rapid ECG, focused assessment, IV access, biomarkers, and prescribed antiplatelet therapy support time-sensitive care. Ambulation during active ischemic symptoms is unsafe.

items.title: A client's observations trend as follows: 0800 BP 126/78, HR 88, RR 18, SpO₂ 97%; 1000 BP 98/60, HR 112, RR 24, SpO₂ 93%; 1200 BP 82/46, HR 132, RR 30, SpO₂ 88%. What is the priority interpretation?
items.content: Progressive hemodynamic and respiratory deterioration requiring immediate escalation.
items.rationale: Falling blood pressure and oxygen saturation with rising heart and respiratory rates indicate worsening perfusion and respiratory compromise. Activate rapid response rather than waiting for routine reassessment.

items.title: A septic client's urine output is 42 mL/hr at 0800, 25 mL/hr at 0900, 14 mL/hr at 1000, and 10 mL/hr at 1100; creatinine rises from 0.9 to 1.8 mg/dL. What should the nurse conclude?
items.content: Renal function and perfusion are worsening; urgent reassessment and escalation are needed.
items.rationale: Progressive oliguria with rising creatinine is concerning for acute kidney injury. Reassess hemodynamics, volume status, nephrotoxic exposures, and escalate promptly.

items.title: A 72-year-old with chronic heart failure reports two days of worsening orthopnea and a 2.4-kg weight gain. Assessment: BP 168/92 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 28/min, SpO₂ 88% on room air, crackles halfway up both lungs, and 3+ ankle edema. Which problem is the priority and what initial nursing actions are indicated?
items.content: Priority: acute pulmonary congestion with hypoxemia. Actions: position upright, provide prescribed oxygen, urgently notify the provider/rapid response based on severity, administer prescribed IV diuretic, and reassess respiratory status and urine output.
items.rationale: The weight gain, edema, crackles, orthopnea, and hypoxemia indicate acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary congestion. Oxygenation and work of breathing take priority while prescribed diuresis and close reassessment address fluid overload.

items.title: A client with a tibial fracture reports escalating pain despite opioid analgesia. The affected foot is tense and pain increases with passive toe movement. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Notify the orthopedic team immediately and prepare for urgent evaluation.
items.rationale: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome. Delay can cause irreversible neurovascular injury.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has an oral temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) and an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm³. What is the priority?
items.content: Initiate the febrile-neutropenia protocol and notify the oncology team immediately.
items.rationale: Fever with profound neutropenia is an oncologic emergency. Cultures and prompt empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobials are time-sensitive.

items.title: A client with myasthenia gravis develops a weak cough, difficulty swallowing, and declining vital capacity. What is the priority concern?
items.content: Impending respiratory failure requiring urgent airway and ventilatory assessment.
items.rationale: Bulbar weakness and declining respiratory capacity can progress rapidly to respiratory failure. Escalate before exhaustion or arrest.

items.title: A client with known adrenal insufficiency has vomiting, severe weakness, BP 78/42 mm Hg, sodium 126 mEq/L, and potassium 5.9 mEq/L. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
items.content: Urgent IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluid resuscitation as prescribed.
items.rationale: Adrenal crisis causes cortisol deficiency, hypotension, hyponatremia, and often hyperkalemia. Steroid replacement and volume resuscitation are urgent.

items.title: During a rapid vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and pruritus over the face and upper torso. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Stop or slow the infusion per protocol, assess the client, and notify the prescriber.
items.rationale: An infusion-related reaction is associated with rapid administration. Assess for airway compromise and hypotension; future doses may require slower infusion and prescribed premedication.

items.title: A prescription reads potassium chloride 10 mEq IV push for a client with hypokalemia. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Do not administer; clarify the prescription because IV potassium must never be given by IV push.
items.rationale: Concentrated potassium given by IV push can cause fatal dysrhythmias. It must be diluted and infused at a controlled rate with appropriate monitoring.

items.title: A pregnant client at 32 weeks has painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. Which assessment should the nurse avoid until placenta location is confirmed?
items.content: Digital vaginal examination.
items.rationale: Placenta previa can cause catastrophic hemorrhage with cervical manipulation. Avoid digital examination until ultrasound excludes previa.

items.title: During labor, a client suddenly develops severe dyspnea, cyanosis, hypotension, and bleeding from IV sites. What should the team suspect?
items.content: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiopulmonary collapse and coagulopathy.
items.rationale: Sudden hypoxia, cardiovascular collapse, and disseminated coagulopathy during labor or shortly after birth are characteristic warning features. Activate emergency multidisciplinary response.

items.title: A 9-month-old has episodic severe crying with knees drawn to the chest, vomiting, and currant-jelly stool. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
items.content: Intussusception.
items.rationale: Intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, and bloody mucus stool are classic findings. Prompt evaluation is needed because bowel ischemia or perforation can occur.

items.title: A 3-year-old has fever for 6 days, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, cracked lips, and swollen hands. Which complication is most important to prevent?
items.content: Coronary artery aneurysm.
items.rationale: Kawasaki disease causes vasculitis with risk of coronary artery involvement. Timely IV immunoglobulin and aspirin therapy are used under specialist direction.

items.title: A client 18 hours after the last drink develops tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and agitation. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?
items.content: Administer prescribed benzodiazepine using the withdrawal protocol and monitor closely.
items.rationale: Benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal severity and seizure risk. Monitor autonomic instability, mental status, hydration, and progression to delirium tremens.

items.title: A client with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis must leave the room for imaging. What protection should the nurse ensure for transport?
items.content: The client wears a surgical mask during transport; staff use fit-tested respiratory protection as indicated.
items.rationale: The patient wears a surgical mask to reduce droplet nuclei dispersal during transport. Staff entering the airborne isolation room require an appropriate fit-tested respirator.

items.title: A client after cardiac surgery has hypotension, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, and narrowing pulse pressure. What complication should the nurse suspect?
items.content: Cardiac tamponade.
items.rationale: Beck triad and hemodynamic compromise suggest tamponade, which restricts ventricular filling. This requires immediate escalation and likely urgent drainage.

items.title: A client found after prolonged immobilization has muscle pain, dark urine, and markedly elevated creatine kinase. Which actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Administer prescribed isotonic IV fluids; monitor potassium and renal function; measure urine output; assess for dysrhythmias.
items.rationale: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin and potassium, risking acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia. Early fluids and close renal/electrolyte monitoring are central.

items.title: A client is admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Initiate droplet precautions; administer prescribed antimicrobials promptly; monitor neurologic status; assess for signs of increased intracranial pressure.
items.rationale: Meningococcal disease requires droplet precautions until appropriate treatment duration. Prompt antimicrobials and neurologic monitoring reduce morbidity and detect complications.

items.title: A client will take prednisone for several weeks. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Take with food; do not stop prolonged therapy abruptly; report fever or signs of infection; monitor glucose as directed.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids can cause gastrointestinal irritation, immunosuppression, hyperglycemia, and adrenal suppression. Tapering may be required after prolonged use.

items.title: A client with severe preeclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate. Which findings require immediate action? Select all that apply.
items.content: Respiratory rate 9/min; absent deep tendon reflexes; urine output 20 mL over 2 hours.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression, absent reflexes, and oliguria suggest magnesium accumulation and toxicity. Stop the infusion, escalate, support breathing, and prepare prescribed calcium gluconate.

items.title: A toddler has barking cough and inspiratory stridor at rest. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Keep the child calm; administer prescribed dexamethasone; administer nebulized epinephrine for significant stridor; reassess for rebound symptoms.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation. Nebulized epinephrine provides temporary relief in moderate-to-severe croup; observe after treatment for recurrence.

items.title: A client experiencing a panic attack is hyperventilating and says, “I am going to die.” Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Stay with the client; use short, calm statements; reduce environmental stimulation; coach slow breathing when the client can engage.
items.rationale: Presence and calm, simple communication reduce fear and stimulation. Avoid complex teaching during peak panic; assess for medical causes when indicated.

items.title: A client with recurrent seizures is admitted to the unit. Which safety measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Pad side rails per policy; keep suction and oxygen available; maintain a low bed; during a seizure protect the head and turn the client laterally when possible.
items.rationale: Environmental preparation reduces injury and supports airway management. Do not restrain the client or place objects in the mouth during a seizure.

items.title: A client with acute liver failure is confused and has asterixis, rising INR, and hypoglycemia. Select the 3 complications that require close monitoring.
items.content: Encephalopathy progression; bleeding; recurrent hypoglycemia.
items.rationale: Hepatic failure impairs ammonia clearance, clotting factor synthesis, and glucose regulation. Neurologic status, bleeding, and glucose require close monitoring.

items.title: A client with type 1 diabetes using an insulin pump has nausea, glucose 380 mg/dL, and positive blood ketones. Select the 3 immediate actions.
items.content: Check the infusion set and pump for interruption; check electrolytes and acid-base status; initiate the prescribed DKA evaluation and treatment pathway.
items.rationale: Pump users receive only rapid-acting insulin, so interruption can quickly cause ketosis. Evaluate for DKA and restore insulin delivery according to clinical orders.

items.title: A newborn of a diabetic parent is jittery and feeds poorly. Select the 3 priority actions.
items.content: Check bedside blood glucose promptly; assess temperature and respiratory status; initiate prescribed feeding or dextrose treatment based on the result and symptoms.
items.rationale: Jitteriness and poor feeding may indicate neonatal hypoglycemia. Rapid glucose measurement and protocol-based treatment prevent neurologic injury.

items.title: A client with a casted lower leg reports worsening pain. Select the 3 findings most concerning for compartment syndrome.
items.content: Pain unrelieved by analgesia; pain with passive stretch; tense swelling of the compartment.
items.rationale: These are early warning signs of rising compartment pressure. Paresthesia and paralysis are later findings; urgent surgical evaluation is required.

items.title: Match each presentation with the most likely shock type.
items.content: rows:massive gastrointestinal bleeding with cool clammy skin;acute myocardial infarction with pulmonary edema and hypotension;spinal cord injury with hypotension and bradycardia|columns:hypovolemic;cardiogenic;neurogenic|answers:massive gastrointestinal bleeding with cool clammy skin=hypovolemic;acute myocardial infarction with pulmonary edema and hypotension=cardiogenic;spinal cord injury with hypotension and bradycardia=neurogenic
items.rationale: Hemorrhage causes loss of circulating volume. Pump failure after MI causes cardiogenic shock. Loss of sympathetic tone after spinal injury can produce neurogenic shock with bradycardia.

items.title: Match each toxic exposure with its antidote.
items.content: rows:opioid toxicity;acetaminophen overdose;heparin-associated bleeding|columns:naloxone;N-acetylcysteine;protamine sulfate|answers:opioid toxicity=naloxone;acetaminophen overdose=N-acetylcysteine;heparin-associated bleeding=protamine sulfate
items.rationale: Naloxone reverses opioid effects. N-acetylcysteine limits acetaminophen-related hepatic injury. Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin.

items.title: For each stroke-related finding, select all appropriate nursing actions.
items.content: rows:suspected acute stroke before imaging;dysphagia after stroke;new decline in consciousness|columns:establish last-known-well time;keep NPO until swallow screen;activate urgent neurologic reassessment;give oral fluids to test swallowing|answers:suspected acute stroke before imaging=establish last-known-well time,activate urgent neurologic reassessment;dysphagia after stroke=keep NPO until swallow screen;new decline in consciousness=activate urgent neurologic reassessment
items.rationale: Time of onset guides treatment eligibility. Swallow screening is required before oral intake to reduce aspiration. A new neurologic decline requires immediate reassessment and escalation.

items.title: For each risk or finding, select all appropriate preventive responses.
items.content: rows:urinary incontinence;limited mobility;nonblanchable sacral erythema|columns:cleanse and apply moisture barrier;individualized repositioning and heel offloading;pressure redistribution and skin assessment;massage reddened bony prominence|answers:urinary incontinence=cleanse and apply moisture barrier;limited mobility=individualized repositioning and heel offloading,pressure redistribution and skin assessment;nonblanchable sacral erythema=pressure redistribution and skin assessment,individualized repositioning and heel offloading
items.rationale: Moisture management and pressure redistribution reduce tissue injury. Nonblanchable erythema requires offloading and assessment; massage can worsen damaged tissue.

items.title: A client with a positive pregnancy test has unilateral pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, and hypotension. Suspect a ruptured ___. Prioritize assessment for ___ and prepare for urgent ___.
items.content: ectopic pregnancy|hemorrhagic shock|surgical management
items.rationale: Unilateral pain, referred shoulder pain, and hypotension suggest intra-abdominal bleeding from ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Stabilization and urgent surgical management are required.

items.title: An older adult with glucose 920 mg/dL, profound dehydration, and altered mentation may have ___. Initial management includes prescribed ___ fluids and close monitoring of serum ___.
items.content: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state|isotonic|osmolality and electrolytes
items.rationale: HHS causes profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with dehydration. Isotonic fluid resuscitation is initiated, with careful monitoring of sodium, potassium, osmolality, and neurologic status.

items.title: Minutes after receiving an antibiotic, a client develops generalized urticaria, wheezing, lip swelling, and BP 76/40 mm Hg. Select the condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:anaphylaxis|actions:administer IM epinephrine promptly as prescribed or protocol-directed;support airway and oxygenation and activate emergency response|monitor:airway patency and respiratory effort;blood pressure and perfusion
items.rationale: Rapid multisystem symptoms with hypotension after exposure indicate anaphylaxis. IM epinephrine is first-line; airway support and hemodynamic monitoring are essential.

items.title: A 13-year-old with type 1 diabetes has abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations, glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.12, and positive ketones. Select the condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:diabetic ketoacidosis|actions:begin prescribed isotonic fluid resuscitation;initiate IV insulin after confirming potassium is safe|monitor:serum potassium and cardiac rhythm;neurologic status and glucose/ketone trend
items.rationale: The findings establish DKA with acidosis and dehydration. Fluids are initiated; insulin is started only after potassium assessment because insulin can worsen hypokalemia. Monitor electrolytes, rhythm, and neurologic status.

items.title: Highlight the findings in a client taking an SSRI who recently started linezolid that suggest serotonin syndrome: inducible clonus; hyperreflexia; temperature 39.1 °C; isolated dry skin; new agitation and diaphoresis.
items.content: segments:inducible clonus|hyperreflexia|temperature 39.1 C|isolated dry skin|new agitation and diaphoresis|correct:1,2,3,5
items.rationale: Clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, agitation, and diaphoresis after serotonergic drug interaction suggest serotonin syndrome. Stop serotonergic agents as directed and escalate urgently.

items.title: Highlight findings in a client with abdominal pain that require urgent surgical evaluation: rigid boardlike abdomen; rebound tenderness; mild hunger; sudden pain relief followed by hypotension; chronic unchanged constipation.
items.content: segments:rigid boardlike abdomen|rebound tenderness|mild hunger|sudden pain relief followed by hypotension|chronic unchanged constipation|correct:1,2,4
items.rationale: Rigidity and rebound suggest peritoneal irritation. Sudden pain relief followed by hypotension may indicate perforation with deterioration. Urgent surgical assessment is required.

items.title: A client weighs 72 kg and is 1.60 m tall. Calculate BMI to one decimal place.
items.rationale: BMI = weight ÷ height squared = 72 ÷ (1.60 × 1.60) = 28.125, rounded to 28.1 kg/m².

items.title: A medication diluted in 100 mL is prescribed to infuse over 30 minutes. What pump rate should be programmed in mL/hr?
items.rationale: 30 minutes is 0.5 hour. 100 mL ÷ 0.5 hour = 200 mL/hr. Verify drug-specific infusion limits and compatibility.

items.title: Arrange the initial nursing actions for a client with sudden unilateral weakness in priority order.
items.content: Activate the stroke response and note last-known-well time.|Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and bedside glucose.|Prepare for urgent noncontrast head CT and prescribed stroke evaluation.|Maintain NPO status until swallowing safety is assessed.
items.rationale: Stroke activation and time documentation preserve treatment options. Stabilization and glucose assessment identify immediate threats and mimics. CT distinguishes hemorrhage; NPO status reduces aspiration risk.

items.title: Arrange the immediate team response to shoulder dystocia.
items.content: Call for help and announce shoulder dystocia.|Assist the client into McRoberts position.|Apply suprapubic pressure as directed by the obstetric clinician.|Prepare for additional maneuvers and neonatal resuscitation support.
items.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires rapid coordinated maneuvers. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure are initial techniques; fundal pressure must not be used.

items.title: A hospitalized client has rising creatinine after contrast imaging. Select all appropriate nursing actions.
items.content: Review and report nephrotoxic medications; monitor urine output and creatinine; assess volume status and administer prescribed fluids; trend potassium and other electrolytes; restrict all fluids without an order.
items.rationale: Review nephrotoxins, monitor renal function and electrolytes, assess volume, and follow prescribed hydration. Unordered fluid restriction may worsen renal perfusion.

items.title: An older adult hospitalized with infection becomes intermittently disoriented at night. Select all appropriate nursing interventions.
items.content: Provide clocks and familiar orientation cues; promote sleep and daytime mobilization; ensure hearing aids and glasses are available; assess pain, oxygenation, hydration, and medication effects; use restraints routinely to prevent wandering.
items.rationale: Delirium care focuses on identifying reversible causes and nonpharmacologic support. Sensory aids, orientation, sleep, mobility, hydration, and pain control help; routine restraints can worsen agitation.

items.title: A client taking warfarin has INR values of 2.2 on Monday, 3.4 on Wednesday, and 5.8 on Friday, with new gum bleeding. What is the priority interpretation?
items.content: The client has excessive anticoagulation with active bleeding; hold further doses pending urgent prescriber direction and assess for additional bleeding.
items.rationale: A rising INR above the usual therapeutic range with bleeding indicates increased hemorrhage risk. Further dosing requires urgent prescriber review and individualized reversal decisions.

items.title: A postpartum client's fundus changes from firm to boggy; lochia increases from scant to heavy with clots; HR rises from 82 to 126/min and BP falls from 118/74 to 88/52 mm Hg. What is the priority?
items.content: Recognize postpartum hemorrhage and initiate immediate hemorrhage response.
items.rationale: The combination of uterine atony, heavy bleeding, tachycardia, and hypotension indicates significant blood loss. Immediate escalation, uterine massage, quantified blood loss, uterotonics, and resuscitation are required.

items.title: A 5-year-old with fever and vomiting is lethargic. HR 158/min, RR 34/min, BP 78/42 mm Hg, capillary refill 5 seconds, cool extremities, and urine output 0.3 mL/kg/hr. Which condition is most likely and what are the immediate priorities?
items.content: Suspect septic shock. Activate the pediatric sepsis pathway, obtain cultures if this does not delay antimicrobials, administer prescribed isotonic fluid boluses with frequent reassessment, give prompt antimicrobials, and monitor perfusion and urine output.
items.rationale: Hypotension, delayed refill, cool extremities, oliguria, and altered mentation indicate shock. Pediatric resuscitation requires rapid protocol-based fluids and antimicrobials with reassessment for fluid responsiveness and overload.

items.title: An older adult taking digoxin and furosemide reports anorexia, nausea, and yellow halos. HR is 48/min and potassium is 2.9 mEq/L; creatinine has increased from baseline. What is the priority nursing response?
items.content: Withhold digoxin, notify the prescriber urgently, obtain ECG and ordered digoxin/electrolyte/renal studies, and monitor for dysrhythmias.
items.rationale: Bradycardia, visual changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, hypokalemia, and renal impairment strongly suggest digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia and reduced clearance increase risk for serious dysrhythmias.

items.title: A client reports sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 204/110 mm Hg in the right arm and 172/96 mm Hg in the left. What is the priority action?
items.content: Activate emergency evaluation and prepare for rapid blood pressure and heart-rate control as prescribed.
items.rationale: Abrupt tearing pain and unequal arm pressures suggest aortic dissection. This is a vascular emergency requiring urgent imaging and controlled reduction of shear stress.

items.title: A client receiving peritoneal dialysis reports abdominal pain and cloudy effluent. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Notify the dialysis team promptly; collect effluent for cell count and culture as prescribed; assess temperature and abdominal findings; administer prescribed intraperitoneal antimicrobials.
items.rationale: Cloudy dialysate and abdominal pain suggest peritonitis. Prompt specimen collection and antimicrobial treatment are important to preserve peritoneal function and prevent sepsis.

items.title: A client has dysphagia after a stroke. Select the 3 actions that reduce aspiration risk during oral intake.
items.content: Keep the client upright at 90 degrees; follow the prescribed texture and liquid consistency; check for pocketing and maintain upright positioning after meals.
items.rationale: Upright posture, prescribed consistency, and checking for retained food reduce aspiration. Oral intake should begin only after an appropriate swallow assessment.

items.title: Match each finding with the more likely vascular disorder.
items.content: rows:leg pain with walking relieved by rest;brown ankle discoloration with edema;cool foot with diminished pulses|columns:peripheral arterial disease;chronic venous insufficiency|answers:leg pain with walking relieved by rest=peripheral arterial disease;brown ankle discoloration with edema=chronic venous insufficiency;cool foot with diminished pulses=peripheral arterial disease
items.rationale: Intermittent claudication, coolness, and diminished pulses suggest arterial insufficiency. Dependent edema and brown gaiter-area pigmentation are characteristic of chronic venous disease.

items.title: A client with untreated hyperthyroidism has fever 40 °C, severe tachycardia, agitation, and vomiting. Suspect ___. Priority supportive care includes cooling and prescribed ___; monitor for ___ instability.
items.content: thyroid storm|beta blocker and antithyroid therapy|cardiovascular
items.rationale: Thyroid storm is life-threatening thyrotoxicosis. Treatment includes supportive cooling, beta blockade, antithyroid medication, and close cardiovascular monitoring.

items.title: A client with cirrhosis vomits a large amount of bright-red blood and becomes hypotensive and tachycardic. Select the likely condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage|actions:establish large-bore IV access and initiate prescribed resuscitation;prepare for urgent endoscopy and prescribed vasoactive therapy if variceal bleeding is suspected|monitor:hemodynamic status;hemoglobin and ongoing blood loss
items.rationale: Hematemesis with shock in cirrhosis suggests major upper GI bleeding, potentially variceal. Resuscitation and urgent definitive evaluation are required; monitor perfusion and blood loss.

items.title: Highlight findings in a febrile client that suggest meningococcemia and require immediate escalation: rapidly spreading nonblanching petechiae; severe headache and neck stiffness; mild seasonal sneezing; hypotension; cool mottled extremities.
items.content: segments:rapidly spreading nonblanching petechiae|severe headache and neck stiffness|mild seasonal sneezing|hypotension|cool mottled extremities|correct:1,2,4,5
items.rationale: A rapidly spreading purpuric rash, meningismus, hypotension, and poor perfusion can indicate meningococcal sepsis. Immediate isolation, antimicrobials, and resuscitation are essential.

items.title: The prescription is 750 mg. The available tablets contain 250 mg each. How many tablets should the nurse administer?
items.content: 3|tablets|0
items.rationale: 750 mg ÷ 250 mg per tablet = 3 tablets. Verify the formulation and whether the prescribed dose is within the safe range.

items.title: A client taking digoxin has potassium values of 4.1, 3.4, and 2.8 mEq/L over 24 hours and develops nausea and a pulse of 50/min. What is the priority interpretation?
items.content: The client is at increased risk for digoxin toxicity and dysrhythmia; withhold the dose and escalate for urgent evaluation.
items.rationale: Falling potassium increases myocardial sensitivity to digoxin. New nausea and bradycardia are concerning for toxicity and require withholding the dose, ECG assessment, and urgent review.
